To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dairy goat farmers have a high seroprevalance to Coxiella burnetti and that the risk factors for seroconversion are performing three or more goat related tasks, farm location, farm biosecurity measures and farm characteristics.

the prevalence of Coxiella burneti seropositivity was higher among dairy goat farmers, their spouses, and children (12 to 17 years of age) living or working on dairy goat farms than the general population.

dairy goat farmers, their spouses and children living and working on dairy goat farms are at risk of acquiring Q fever and that risk can be reduced by implementing general biosecurity measures and vaccination of seronevative farmers and their household.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the seroprevelence of Q fever in goat farmers and their families and the risk factors for seroconversion.
the risk of Q fever for the farmers and their households, which is an important aspect of the Q fever epidemic.
a zoonotic disease, Q fever, that can have severe health consequences for the farmers and their household, but also for the general population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk for farmers, spouses, and children of dairy goat farmers to be exposed to Q fever is high.
Q fever is a serious health threat to goat farmers and their households and that a multifaceted control strategy is required to prevent further transmission.
the current Q fever vaccination policy is not effective enough to prevent human infection and that a more effective policy should be developed and implemented.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Q fever seroprevalences among goat farmers, their spouses and their children are high.
the risk of Q fever in goat farmers and their households is high, but that the disease can be prevented by vaccination of the small ruminants.
the risk of Q fever infection is very high for farmers and their family members living or working in a goat farm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Q fever seroprevalences were high in dairy goat farmers, spouses, and their children living and working on these farms in 2009–10.

dairy goat farmers and household members are at a high risk to become infected with C. burnetii, which can cause severe sequelae.
